o: Longest contiguous subarray whose first element is strictly greater than its last. Equivalently, for each i find the farthest j > i with nums[j] < nums[i] and maximize j − i + 1. Example 2: from 61 (index 4) the farthest smaller element to its right is 60 (index 9), giving length 6. Sorting by value and sweeping lets each element query 'max index among strictly smaller values' in O(1) amortized.
k: Answer = max over i of (farthest right index with a strictly smaller value) − i + 1.
Process values ascending while maintaining the max index seen among strictly smaller values; handle equal-value groups together (equal values can't pair).
Brute force with early exit is a fine intuition builder but degrades to O(n²).

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Early Exit
a.i: For each start i, scan j from the right end leftward and stop at the first nums[j] < nums[i]. Worst case O(n²) (e.g., decreasing array finds instantly, but adversarial inputs scan far), acceptable conceptually, risky at n = 1e5.
s: For each i from 0 to n−1, scan j from n−1 down to i+1.
If nums[j] < nums[i], update the answer with j − i + 1 and break.
Return the best length (0 if none).
a.t: O(n²) worst case — inner scan may run long for many starts

a.n: Approach 2: Sort by Value Ascending + Running Max Index
a.i: Sort (value, index) pairs ascending. Sweeping in this order, when we reach value v at index i, every previously processed index holds a strictly smaller value; the maximum such index is the best j for i. Equal values are batched: answer queries first (using only strictly smaller values), then fold the group's indices into the running max. Length is maxIdx − i + 1.
s: Create (value, index) pairs and sort ascending by value.
Sweep groups of equal value: for each index i in the group, if a strictly smaller value was seen, update ans with maxIdx − i + 1.
After the group, set maxIdx = max(maxIdx, group's max index).
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the sweep is linear

w: The sort-and-sweep is the interview winner: reframe 'farthest smaller element to the right' as 'max index among strictly smaller values' and batch ties. Pitfalls: using ≥ instead of strict inequality when pairing (equal endpoints don't count), and the +1 in the length formula. Follow-ups: count semi-decreasing subarrays, or answer for 'first ≥ last' (symmetric sweep descending).
